questiontext.text: <p>Why do scholarly digital editions strictly separate encoded textual content from presentation stylesheets?</p>

answer.text: <p>Keeping the look in display rules means editors can update, redesign, or reformat presentation without touching or risking the primary textual evidence.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Separating content from presentation ensures that evidence remains fixed and reproducible while display stylesheets can evolve independently.</p>

answer.text: <p>Web browsers refuse to parse XML files that contain any visual styling instructions.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Browsers can apply styling via CSS or XSLT, but mixing display directives with semantic encoding violates digital humanities standards.</p>

answer.text: <p>TEI schemas automatically delete any XML file that specifies font sizes or margin widths.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Schemas validate element containment and attribute constraints; they do not delete files.</p>

answer.text: <p>Print publishers require all digital files to be monochrome before peer review.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Digital editions support multi-modal publication across color web screens and print formats.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>How does a single normalized TEI XML document support both a diplomatic view and a modernized reading view?</p>

answer.text: <p>The stylesheet selectively activates different child elements within TEI &lt;choice&gt; containers (displaying &lt;orig&gt; for diplomatic views and &lt;reg&gt; for reading views).</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. The &lt;choice&gt; container encapsulates alternative layers, allowing stylesheets to toggle between verbatim witness evidence and normalized reading text.</p>

answer.text: <p>The editor must maintain two separate XML files in different Git repositories.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Maintaining duplicate files causes version drift; a single TEI file holds both layers simultaneously.</p>

answer.text: <p>A machine learning model rewrites the text dynamically on the fly each time a student visits the page.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Scholarly editions rely on deterministic, editorially verified markup rather than live non-deterministic AI regeneration.</p>

answer.text: <p>Diplomatic views require specialized hardware monitors that cannot display modern fonts.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Both views are rendered in standard web browsers using standard CSS and web typography.</p>

name.text: 03 Question: Milestone Line Breaks and Word Boundaries

questiontext.text: <p>Why must stylesheet rules for milestone line breaks (&lt;lb/&gt;) be carefully audited for whitespace handling?</p>

answer.text: <p>A naive line-break rule that outputs a line break without a trailing or leading space will glue the last word of a line to the first word of the next line, unless &lt;lb break="no"/&gt; is specified.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Milestone line breaks replace physical line breaks; omitting spaces on standard breaks merges adjacent words into unreadable strings.</p>

answer.text: <p>Browsers automatically crash when encountering self-closing XML milestone elements.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Modern XML parsers and custom element processors handle self-closing tags without issue.</p>

answer.text: <p>Line break elements permanently delete all vowels from preceding words during transformation.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Line breaks mark physical layout transitions; they do not alter lexical tokens.</p>

answer.text: <p>HTML does not support line breaks in paragraphs.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. HTML supports &lt;br&gt; and CSS block line-breaking.</p>

name.text: 04 Question: Browser Treatment of Custom TEI Elements

questiontext.text: <p>When a modern browser renders custom elements generated by CETEIcean (e.g., &lt;tei-p&gt; or &lt;tei-div&gt;), what is its default layout behavior before custom CSS is applied?</p>

answer.text: <p>Browsers treat unknown custom elements as inline elements (display: inline), requiring explicit CSS rules (display: block) to establish structural paragraph blocks.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. The HTML specification treats unregistered custom elements as inline by default; CSS must explicitly declare structural blocks.</p>

answer.text: <p>Browsers immediately hide all custom elements with display: none.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Browsers render unknown elements inline rather than hiding them.</p>

answer.text: <p>Browsers automatically format &lt;tei-p&gt; with standard 16px paragraph margins and line breaks.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. HTML user-agent stylesheets only style native HTML elements (like &lt;p&gt;), not custom custom elements.</p>

answer.text: <p>Browsers throw a fatal security exception and halt JavaScript execution.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Custom elements are fully valid in HTML5 and DOM specifications.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>In an XSLT stylesheet, what is the primary function of the &lt;xsl:apply-templates/&gt; instruction inside a matched template?</p>

answer.text: <p>It instructs the transformation processor to recursively process the child nodes of the current element using the stylesheet's matching rules.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. &lt;xsl:apply-templates/&gt; drives recursive descent through the XML tree, applying the appropriate template rules to child elements.</p>

answer.text: <p>It compiles the XML file into an executable binary program.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. XSLT is a declarative tree-transformation language, not a binary compiler.</p>

answer.text: <p>It sends an automated email notification to the repository administrator.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. XSLT templates process XML node hierarchies.</p>

answer.text: <p>It permanently overwrites the input XML source file with raw HTML.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. XSLT takes an input tree and produces an output tree, leaving the source file untouched.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>How does the CETEIcean JavaScript library render TEI documents without requiring server-side XSLT transformation?</p>

answer.text: <p>It loads TEI XML directly into the browser DOM, prefixing elements with 'tei-' to create valid HTML5 custom elements that are styled directly with standard CSS.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. CETEIcean imports TEI XML into the browser DOM as custom elements, allowing direct CSS styling and client-side behavioral attachment.</p>

answer.text: <p>It converts all XML text into raster PNG screenshots before display.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. CETEIcean produces live, accessible, searchable DOM text elements.</p>

answer.text: <p>It runs a full headless Ubuntu Linux virtual machine inside the web browser.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. CETEIcean is a lightweight JavaScript library that manipulates DOM elements directly.</p>

answer.text: <p>It translates the TEI file into Markdown and parses it with Python.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. CETEIcean operates entirely in browser-side JavaScript without Python runtime dependencies.</p>

name.text: 07 Question: Local HTTP Server Requirement for CETEIcean

questiontext.text: <p>Why must a local CETEIcean HTML file be opened through a web server (such as Python's http.server) rather than by double-clicking the file (file:///)?</p>

answer.text: <p>Browser security models block JavaScript fetch() requests to local file:/// URLs under the Same-Origin Policy (CORS), preventing the script from reading the XML file.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Browser security restrictions block client-side fetch requests to local file system paths, requiring an HTTP server origin.</p>

answer.text: <p>Custom CSS files can only be downloaded from remote cloud servers.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. CSS can be served locally; the restriction specifically applies to JavaScript fetch() on file:/// URLs.</p>

answer.text: <p>Python http.server is required to compile XML into C++ before the browser can understand it.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Browsers parse XML natively; the server simply fulfills HTTP GET requests.</p>

answer.text: <p>Local files are encrypted by the operating system until an HTTP handshake occurs.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Local file permissions are governed by the OS, but browser security sandbox rules enforce CORS restrictions on fetch.</p>

name.text: 08 Question: First-Child Assumptions in AI-Generated Stylesheets

questiontext.text: <p>What common architectural error do AI models frequently introduce when asked to write XSLT rules for TEI &lt;choice&gt; containers?</p>

answer.text: <p>Selecting child elements by position (e.g. *[1]) rather than by element name (e.g. tei:reg), causing silent failures whenever markup order or child types vary.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Assuming that the regularized reading is always the first child creates brittle rules that break whenever &lt;orig&gt; or comments precede &lt;reg&gt;.</p>

answer.text: <p>Assuming that &lt;choice&gt; can only contain audio recordings.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. AI models recognize &lt;choice&gt; as textual, but frequently assume a rigid child sequence.</p>

answer.text: <p>Replacing all &lt;choice&gt; tags with SQL database table queries.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. The issue is XPath selector specificity, not database injection.</p>

answer.text: <p>Refusing to generate XSLT because TEI is considered deprecated.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. AI models readily generate XSLT, but often rely on fragile positional selectors.</p>

name.text: 09 Question: Whitespace Normalization Traps in Mixed Content

questiontext.text: <p>Why is applying the XSLT normalize-space() function indiscriminately across an entire document hazardous in scholarly editions?</p>

answer.text: <p>In mixed content (text interleaved with inline tags), normalize-space() strips leading and trailing spaces around inline elements, gluing adjacent words together.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. normalize-space() removes boundary whitespace; when applied to inline elements like &lt;persName&gt; or &lt;hi&gt;, it fuses them with surrounding prose.</p>

answer.text: <p>normalize-space() permanently converts all uppercase letters to lowercase.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. normalize-space() only collapses whitespace; it does not alter letter case.</p>

answer.text: <p>The function causes XML parsers to run out of memory on files larger than 10 lines.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. normalize-space() is a lightweight string processing function.</p>

answer.text: <p>It converts all spaces into hexadecimal numbers.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. It strips leading/trailing spaces and collapses internal whitespace to single spaces.</p>

name.text: 10 Question: The Four-Part Stylesheet Audit Framework

questiontext.text: <p>In Lesson 7.3's human-in-the-loop audit framework, which sequence of verification steps ensures that an AI-generated stylesheet satisfies scholarly fidelity?</p>

answer.text: <p>1) Execution check (does it run); 2) Template inspection; 3) Word-by-word diff against manual ground truth (compare.py); 4) Element count audit (count.py).</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. The four-part framework verifies basic execution, inspects template logic, catches silent text omissions or corruptions via text diff, and verifies element counts.</p>

answer.text: <p>1) Prompting the model twice; 2) Accepting the second output without checking.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Unchecked AI output violates basic digital humanities reproducibility and rigor.</p>

answer.text: <p>1) Running a spell-check in Microsoft Word; 2) Uploading directly to Moodle.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Spell checks do not evaluate XML structural mapping or stylesheet fidelity.</p>

answer.text: <p>1) Converting the stylesheet to PDF; 2) Printing on paper; 3) Shredding the original.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Digital scholarship requires rigorous algorithmic and textual auditing.</p>
